In general, the mechanistic underpinnings of anthropogenically mitigated disease emergence are poorly understood; dynamic, spatial models could help elucidate this gap in understanding. In a time of rapidly increasing human-mediated changes to the environment, understanding the ramifications of habitat fragmentation, human disturbance, urbanization and climate change on pathogen transmission is critical. In the future, spatial models for wildlife may also be helpful in linking the effects of climate on pathogen transmission across multiple scales. There is room for additional synthesis between the realms of movement and disease ecology, where the results of statistical movement models can be used to generate rule-based movement to better infer realistic contact patterns. Moving forward, better integration of individual-based disease models and statistical movement models that take into account the “internal state” of the animal could provide new insights. In general, more mechanistic models of long-distance migration are needed (Bauer & Hoye, 2014; Galsworthy et al., 2011), especially since human-mediated changes to the environment may dramatically alter or impede migration patterns for vulnerable species. Since the relative importance of local and long-distance processes is often unknown for pathogen transmission in wildlife, landscape genetic approaches like isolation by distance and spatial assignment can provide important information about levels of connectivity between different populations, and thus provide  inferences about rates of migration and dispersal. Further utilization of such landscape genetic and genomic techniques could help with the challenges of parameterization (Archie & Theis, 2011), elucidate who-transmits-to-whom (Morelli et al., 2012), and could enable the testing of new hypotheses about spatial spread and connectivity that were previously untestable (Cowled et al., 2012). An important next step for spatial, individual-based models might be to incorporate feedbacks between behaviour and physiology, such as sickness-induced behavioural changes or variable transmission efficiency between populations. In the future, it may also be useful to explore the relative importance of spatial heterogeneity in determining outcomes by comparing results with an equivalent non-spatial model for more host–pathogen systems (e.g., Bar-David et al., 2006; Marion, Smith, Swain, Davidson, & Hutchings, 2008). In addition, sensitivity analyses should be used to identify parameters that are most critical to predicting disease dynamics or that should be prioritized for future data collection or monitoring (e.g., Goyens et al., 2013; Highfield, Ward, Laffan, Norby, & Wagner, 2010b). Another challenge and important area for future research is determining the scale at which pathogen transmission should be estimated and modelled. In general, meta-models may prove to be a powerful tool for representing dynamic and complex spatial patterns in wildlife disease systems where multiple processes occur at competing scales. While some of the research gaps identified in this review can be addressed by broadening taxonomic foci and integrating  knowledge across disciplines, we also need to identify commonalities among different disease systems and specify the scale and intensity of data required to adequately model management-relevant questions.
